subject: Cognitive Science
title: Nudge Architecture
description: Learn Nudge Architecture in one minute.

hook.text: Put fruit at eye level in a cafeteria and sales jump 25%. No ban, no lecture—just architecture.

buildup.text: Nudge architecture designs choice environments to steer better decisions without removing any options.

discovery.text: Thaler and Sunstein call it libertarian paternalism: influence choices by changing defaults and context.

twist.text: Critics call it manipulation. But every environment nudges—there's no neutral arrangement of choices.

climax.text: Opt-out retirement savings, smaller default plates, and smart form designs have saved billions and lives.

punchline.text: Design the choice, shape the outcome.

quiz.question: What is a nudge in behavioral science?
options: Steering decisions through choice design without removing options

details.summary: Nudge architecture designs choice environments to guide people toward better decisions without restricting freedom. Placing healthy food at eye level, making retirement savings automatic, and defaulting to organ donation opt-out are all nudges that exploit cognitive biases for beneficial outcomes.
details.whyItMatters: Nudge architecture harnesses biases rather than fighting them. It is the most scalable approach to improving decisions across millions of people with minimal effort.
takeaways: Nudges guide decisions through choice environment design
They exploit biases like status quo and default effects
Thaler and Sunstein popularized the concept

faq.question: What is the ethical concern with nudging?
faq.answer: Critics argue nudges are paternalistic manipulation, deciding for people what is in their best interest. Defenders counter that every choice environment has a design, and nudging makes that design intentional rather than accidental. Transparency about nudges helps address ethical concerns.

faq.question: What makes a nudge different from a mandate?
faq.answer: A nudge preserves freedom of choice. People can always opt out. A mandate removes the choice entirely. Making savings automatic with an opt-out is a nudge. Requiring savings contributions is a mandate. The distinction matters for both ethics and political acceptance.
